subtopic: MR. FORTIN-ALLEGED THREATS AGAINST MEMBER FOR TEMISCAMINGUE BY CHAIRMAN OF THE C.B.C.
MR. FORTIN-ALLEGED THREATS AGAINST MEMBER FOR TEMISCAMINGUE BY CHAIRMAN OF THE C.B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like at this time of the business of the House to raise a question of privilege in accordance with the Standing Orders.
We were amazed, my colleagues and I, to read an article in the January 28 edition of the newspaper Le Jour, in the January 27 edition of La Presse and in the January 28 edition of Le Droit, according to which the chairman of a Crown corporation-in this case, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-thundered threats at a member of this House, should the latter not act in such or such a way. I contend, very humbly, that the privileges of this House and of its committees were seriously infringed upon by this senior officer. As a matter of fact, Canadian Broadcasting Corporation Chairman Laurent Picard stated, and I quote:
Federal member of Parliament Real Caouette will have to give proof of his bribery charges against certain newsmen, otherwise he will be hearing from the CBC management.
The chairman of that public corporation, Mr. Laurent Picard, made this statement himself during the weekend to a reporter of the Montreal newspaper La Presse. Mr. Picard added the following:
The CBC's information policy is one of the best and of the most open in the world and one where political interferences are practically non-existent.
Besides, and I wish to draw the attention of the Chair to this, he stated firmly that they would not be accepted.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, that is exactly what Mr. Picard is doing himself as regards the powers and privileges of Parliament and its committees. I call it pure and simple interference on his part. He anticipates the work of the committee. Even if the hon. member for Temis-camingue (Mr. Caouette) was to appear before the committee, as the House would like him to, according to the majority vote registered on December 19 in this House, the hon. member for Temiscamingue is convicted beforehand, he is seriously prejudiced against in the public opinion on account of the statements by the CBC chairman.
But the situation is still more serious, Mr. Speaker. Indeed, the chairman of this Crown corporation, who is not unbiased in this quarrel since he is the chairman of this Crown corporation, some of whose newsmen may be concerned, uttered many serious threats, and I quote him again:
"Mr. Caouette, in the opinion of chairman Picard, is now cornered, as he must appear before long before a committee of the House of
Commons to explain the charges he made in Parliament. He will have to give names and details ...
And one can see to what degree blackmailing may go.
... otherwise the CBC management is willing to reply publicly".
Mr. Speaker, hon. members know that the Standing Orders concerning a question of privilege was devised so as to allow Parliament and its members to discharge their duties without inconvenience, without obstruction of any kind. I contend, with my colleagues, that the hon. member for Temiscamingue will not be at ease to appear before the parliamentary committee as long as such a threat from a Crown corporation exists, a corporation that is itself involved in a conflict which Parliament itself wished to settle by referring it to one of its committees. The objectiveness of the committee's inquiry, with its present mandate, has been reached. Whatever may happen, Mr. Speaker, will the leader of the Social Credit Party of Canada have the same facilities as Mr. Laurent Picard to give explanations through this public corporation whose operation is paid with our taxes?
This is shameless blackmail, Mr. Speaker, against a member of this House. The privilege protecting this House is designed to protect the authority and dignity of Parliament, and protect members against excessive or outside intimidation and pressures. The privilege of this House is to vest Parliament with the power to punish severely those who hold it in contempt, or seek to interfere with its members in the performance of their duties.
Before the committee appointed by the House even sits, the chairman of a Crown corporation condemns the alleged accused. He judges him publicly and causes him a serious prejudice before the whole people of this country. By this threats he wants to force a member to do something that he alone can do under the rules of this House.
As things stand now, Mr. Speaker, no matter what he says before the Committee on Privileges and Elections, the hon. member for Temiscamingue stands condemned by a government official who heads newsmen who could themselves be implicated in this conflict and this inquiry. That, and I say so openly, reaches the highest level of blackmail and conflict of interest.
While saying that the hon. member for Temiscamingue will have to say such and such a thing, or the management of the CBC will take the necessary steps to force him to talk, that corporation arrogates itself a right which it does not have and which belongs only to Parliament. Mr. Speaker, Mr. Picard is guilty of intimidation, excessive pressures outside the House, and flagrant conflict of interest. That is abuse of power!
Will the hon. member for Temiscamingue have the same possibility as CBC to use the air to give his version of the

January 29, 1975
Privilege-Mr. Fortin
matter? Can the Chair give such an assurance to the hon. member for Temiscamingue? Judging by the honesty the CBC has shown for the Social Credit Party in the past there can be very serious doubts about it.
The privileges of this House are seriously prejudiced by a senior official who is an agent of this House under the legislation regulating that corporation. Indeed, that corporation is nothing more than a creation of this Parliament, and it is that corporation created by this Parliament which now wants to dictate what hon. members will do and threatens with reprisals the hon. member or members involved.
Mr. Speaker, Mr. Picard even went much further when he actually said, and I quote:
And even if Mr. Caouette elected to refuse to appear before the parliamentary committee the CBC would try to make him understand that accusations cannot be made like that without rhyme or reason without supporting evidence.
However, Mr. Speaker, that is exactly what the Chairman of the CBC is doing. He accuses and condemns the Leader of the Social Credit Party before the hon. member is even heard by a committee of the House, and following a majority vote by the House.
If this House accepts the CBC statements without retorting, there is no point for the hon. member for Temiscamingue to appear before the committee since he already stands condemned, as I said, to bear the brunt of the CBC with which he is threatened. Somehow that reminds me of justice today which allows bandits to roam around without any threat of capital punishment, and honest people to be the victims of meddling by those who hold key positions.
I say on behalf of my colleagues of the Social Credit Party that the privileges of this House are seriously prejudiced by the fact that the Chairman of a Crown corporation speaks publicly outside the House of things of which the House has not yet disposed.

subtopic: MR. FORTIN-ALLEGED THREATS AGAINST MEMBER FOR TEMISCAMINGUE BY CHAIRMAN OF THE C.B.C.
speechtext:
I have almost finished my remarks, Mr. Speaker. Thus making the public believe in the guilt of a man who has not been judged by his peers yet and who has not even been summoned yet.
This is a most serious offence as it has been committed by a senior official highly paid with taxpayers' money. The president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, a federal official, spoke too much. He has judged, indicted and convicted a member of Parliament. He even arrogates himself the right to use the broadcasting media to threaten a member of this House. If this House permits such threats, this will create a precedent and any obscure civil servant will be able to accuse and threaten a member of Parliament who will have no right to answer through the same broadcasting media and the same means, as the media are controlled by the same person who makes such allegations without any evidence. The President of the CBC bypasses the committee of the House, blackmails an hon. member threatening him to shed light on this matter

through the broadcasting media which are taxpayer-financed. This shows the honesty of the CBC!
Mr. Speaker, to conclude, for the hon. member for Temiscamingue to appear before the committee-and I weigh my words-without any danger of reprisals, and for him to comply with the motion agreed to by this House on December 19th, it will be necessary, and it is a sine qua non requirement, that the President of the CBC be called before the committee'on privileges and elections, that he take back his threats and apologize to the hon. member of Temiscamingue and, furthermore, he will have to guarantee that the CBC will remain neutral in this conflict where it is itself involved.
If the committee on privileges and elections wish to hear witnesses, they will have to be protected against threats.
Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau):
That the President of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation be called before the parliamentary committee on privileges and elections as a witness to take back his words, to apologize to the hon. member for Temiscamingue and to guarantee that neither himself nor the corporation will interfere in the present conflict, neither directly nor indirectly, and to explain what were the allegations of the CBC.

maintopic: DELAY IN THE DELIVERY OF FRENCH EDITION OF HANSARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rose yesterday on a question of privilege to the effect that the French edition of Hansard was issued far too late on the following day to French speaking members.
Now, today, January 29, 1975, at noon sharp, the French copy of the Tuesday, January 28 1975 Hansard had not yet been delivered to my office.
I do not wish to incriminate or blame anyone for their carelessness. I am also aware that the House of Commons civil servants have a sometimes difficult task to carry out and that they cannot deliver copies of the Hansard and other parliamentary documents as long as the printing services have not yet made them available for distribution. Even in the printing service, I know everyone is doing his
January 29, 1975

best and they sometimes operate under conditions and at hours that might be described as inhuman.
However, in the past, when the French copy of the Hansard came in late, it was usually argued that they delay was due to the fact that several French speaking members had taken part in the debate and it took much more time than usual to translate their speeches, and I am quite willing to accept this as a valid reason; bearing that in mind as well as the fact that on Monday, January 27 there was only limited participation by French speaking members in the debates, since I was the only one in my party who did, that is apparently no valid justification for the delay in delivering the French edition of Hansard.
Considering, Mr. Speaker, that on Wednesday, January 29 1975 at noon sharp the French edition of Hansard had not yet been delivered to my office, I am justified in wondering very seriously what is wrong with the printing and delivery. If the translation services are understaffed, I think it might be possible to hire some additional translators.
Mr. Speaker, I am now referring to a decision held yesterday by the Chair to the effect that during the question period members and parties represented in this House draw the attention of the Chair to be recognized so that all questions to be asked by members will be justified.
I am now referring to section 17, page 14, of Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms. Here is how it reads:
Every member as soon as he is chosen becomes a representative of the whole body of the Commons, without any distinction of the place from whence he is sent to Parliament... that every member is equally a representative of the whole has been the constant notion and language of Parliament. Every member, though chosen by one particular district, when elected and returned, serves for the whole realm.
He does not serve for a party, he serves for the whole realm. That is what is found in Beauchesne's I quote again:
For the end of his coming thither is not particular, but general, not barely to advantage his constituents, but the commonwealth.
And that is what I intend to do in this House, according to Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms.
Consequently, because of the facts I have just pointed out, that is the privileges of all members, French-speaking or English-speaking, we are entitled to the same services, the same privileges, we have the same duties and I firmly intend to serve my country, Mr. Speaker, without any discrimination on the basis of race, religion or language.
Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau):
That this House authorize the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization to consider the late distribution of the French edition of the Debates, and make appropriate recommendations in order that the Speaker of the House and his entire staff be in a position to comply with the rights of French-speaking members as well as English-speaking members.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REPLACEMENT OF MONTREAL COMPUTER-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity.
Whereas the only computerized system for paying unemployment benefits in the whole of the province of Quebec is located in Montreal, and whereas the UIC employees report that the computer is almost always out of order, and unable to process benefit payments on time, and considering the constant growth of unemployment in Canada, more especially in Quebec, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin):
That a second paying computer be put into operation in Montreal and that additional computer technicians be hired to ensure the uninterrupted operation of the computer system in order that the thousands of unemployment insurance recipients be no longer penalized on account of the non-operation of the one existing computer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion on a matter which is most certainly of an urgent and pressing necessity since it relates to an industry employing many workers, namely the textile industry.
Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau):
That this House authorize the standing committee or finance, trade and economic affairs to examine without any delay the total impact on the Canadian industry of our imports of textile products and also to investigate the possible relationship between those imports and the lay offs in the textile industry in Quebec.

With all due respect to the Chair, and God knows how I like to go along with the Standing Orders, I would like to point and that at the beginning of this session, in the performance of my duties

Freight Rate Freeze
as a member of this House, I requested unanimous consent, under Standing Order 43, and I asked that any member, opposing unanimous consent for a motion put under the Standing Orders of the House, be assured that the question would be solved so that our procedures and rules be respected. So, any member objecting to such a motion made under Standing Order 43, should necessarily, pursuant to our rules, express his opposition, would it be only by a word, generally by a very clear "no". Our Standing Orders stipulate that when a member seeks the floor, he must first take his hat off although it is a little old-fashioned to require us to do so since we have none, and ask the Chair for permission to speak. At that time, the Chair had heard the very appropriate remarks of the hon. member for Bellechasse and had stated that it would study them very carefully in the light of the Standing Orders of this House.
We are now nearly in February. I am convinced that the Chair has considered the representations made by the hon. member for Bellechasse. I am convinced that, in all honesty, it is ready to make a decision on the observance of this Standing Order in particular. In closing, I would like to ask the Chair if in the days to come the members of this House will be made aware of your decision so that in the future we may act accordingly and follow your decisions.

subsubtopic: REQUEST VAL D'OR BASE BE RE-OPENED-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 43, I request unanimous consent of the House to debate a case of urgent and pressing necessity.
The Canadian forces airport at Val-d'Or was recently closed by the Department of National Defence. Hundreds of families in the Val-d'Or area depend on armed forces activities for their livelyhood. The shutting down of this air force base is causing hardship to a number of businesses. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard):
That th's House request the Minister of National Defense to consider reopening the Canadian Forces base at Val-d'Or, and that the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence be asked to investigate the possibility of reactivating the base, which is vital to the economy of Quebec's northwest.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED MEASURE TO COMBAT INFLATION-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 43, I request unanimous consent of the House to raise a point of special significance requesting immediate attention.
Since inflation rages in our economy and constantly reduces the dollar's real purchasing power, and since increases reach critical proportions requiring urgent measures to prevent total destruction of our economy and society, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette):
January 29, 1975

That this House strongly urge the Minister of Finance to study with utmost speed Bill C-328, an Act to provide for emergency measures to deal with inflation of prices, and also to initiate as soon as possible implementation of measures put forward in that legislation proposed by the hon. member for Temiscamingue. Measures proposed in that bill are adequate to stop the havoc of inflation.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR AID TO VICTIMS OF LANDSLIDE AT ASBESTOS, QUEBEC-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to discuss a very urgent and important matter.
In view of the serious landslides which occurred and are still occurring near the crater of the Canadian John's Manville's mine at Asbestos, sweeping along whole houses and buildings into the mine and leaving more than 80 families homeless, and since the situation represents a serious threat to the security of citizens as well as an excessive financial burden for the municipality of Asbestos which must relocate in a very short time a whole section of the town, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin):
That the House of Commons be allowed to discuss now the possibility that the federal government, in cooperation with the provincial government and the town of Asbestos, might provide some assistance to the citizens affected by the disaster, help relocate them and take part, if necessary, in the permanent establishment of a really safe buffer area.

Mr. Speaker, I would not want the war that has been started to turn into an internal war within Parliament. I would not want that at all and I would be the last man to fight in such a war.
However, with regard to the question of privilege that has just been raised, I have felt singled out as the member for Bellechasse because of the remarks I made yesterday, and even the corrections I made and the motion I moved. About the question of privilege I raised today, I could not accept that as a complete Canadian in my country when the French network of the CBC has been showing for three weeks the french version of "The Great Challenge" through which everyone in Canada can witness the debates that took place in this House on the construction of a railway in Western Canada.
I have tried, Mr. Speaker, with all the good faith of a 100 per cent Canadian, to understand the purpose of those debates, the interventions of each member, be he a Liberal, Progressive Conservative, or an Independent. I understood that all those hon. members were considering Canada's future, greatness and development. That is what I understood. On January 28, January 29 and tomorrow, if necessary, the hon. member for Bellechasse will perform his duty. We have privileges in this House, and I feel humiliated at the fact that certain hon. members misunderstand our interventions today which are in order.
We make them, as in the times of Macdonald and all the others, for our rights in this Parliament and in this country to be recognized.
Mr. Speaker, we are going through difficult times. We need an undomitable courage as French-speaking Canadians in this country and in this Parliament to take a stand in face of that wave of separatism we are now experiencing.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say this: whether we are understood, whether the fact that we are French-speaking or English-speaking is understood, we want the rights and privileges of each and everyone to be respected in this House. If we sometimes use steps that are beyond the general understanding of some hon. members, that is not our fault. Personally, I will continue to fight to live in Canada in total freedom and in the respect of this institution.

subsubtopic: METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext: Has the government any plans through the method of special grants to assist school boards in local municipalities and cities to cover costs conversion to the metric system?

speakeroldname: Mr. Gaston Clermont (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext:
The policy of the government in regard to metric conversion was outlined in the White Paper on Metric Conversion laid before the House in January 1970 and approved by the leaders of all parties. Throughout this white paper the analysis is based on the assumption that the costs of conversion will be borne by those incurring them, just as the benefits flowing from conversion will accrue to the individual organizations, either directly or through the general health of the economy. In the case of education the responsibility for costs is in the jurisdiction of the provinces. To the extent that there may be in some cases an unreasonable burden placed on the budgets of individual school divisions this is primarily a responsibility of the province to meet. However, the benefits that the program of metric conversion will bring to the general health of the economy will be experienced by the provinces and to the same extent as by the Federal Government.

Order Paper Questions DECREASE IN STOCK MARKET

subsubtopic: METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext:
1.	Is the government aware that, despite suggestions that company profits have increased, the majority of Canadian company shareholders have seen the stock market value of their holdings decrease by an average of 40 per cent in the past few months?
2.	Is the government considering indexing the capital gains tax, so that shareholders investing in the economy of their country are not obliged to pay taxes on gains resulting from inflation rather than on real appreciation of value?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext: Taxation of capital gains is an issue that is under continuing review. The government has implemented a wide range of measures to combat the inflation rate which is one of the principal causes of the weakness in the stock market values. For Canadians, indexing is a relatively new concept, and it is too early to assess its overall impact from either a tax or economic point of view. We will be in a better position to determine the applicability of other forms of indexing once we have gained more experience with our initial steps with this concept. In applying the current taxation rate on capital gains, the government takes into account the following facts: (1) The capital gains tax is a component of necessary government revenues. A decrease in the capital gains tax would require a corresponding increase in some other area of our tax system. (2) At the time of tax reform, it was decided that only one-half of capital gains would be taxable, partially in recognition that a portion of capital appreciation is a result of inflation and not real growth. (3) To a limited extent, capital gains are currently indexed as the tax brackets for individuals are increased annually to adjust for inflation and one-half of capital gains are included in the computation of personal income. (4) Depreciable as well as non-depreciable capital assets would have to be indexed and this would cause major problems for the taxation of depreciable assets. At the present time, the Department of Finance has undertaken a study of the capital cost allowance system which includes consideration of the impact of inflation on depreciable capital property.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL CENTRAL INFORMATION OFFICE
speechtext: Did the Minister of Finance indicate on January 15, 1973 that the federal and provincial governments are working towards the establishment of a central information centre with the intention of providing, at one central point, information on the borrowing requirements of federal and provincial governments and, if so, what progress has been made?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL CENTRAL INFORMATION OFFICE
speechtext: On January 15, 1973 the Minister of Finance, in reply to a question from the Leader of the Opposition, indicated that in his meetings with provincial finance ministers the previous June, an agreement had been made to create a centralized information system which would gather information on the borrowing intentions of provincial governments and the federal government. The subject of a borrowing information system was discussed at the January 18, 1973 meeting of Ministers of Finance and Provincial Treasurers. At that time, it was reported that progress on the information gathering system had begun and that discussions with provinces had taken place in establishing the technical basis for the system. Further technical work was undertaken during 1973 and provinces submitted their borrowing intentions on the newly-established technical basis in time for the January, 1974 meeting of Ministers of Finance and Provincial Treasurers. During 1974, more technical federal-provincial discussions were under-taken to further refine the system. This culminated in a collection of information in November 1974 and a preparation of a summary borrowing report for 1974-75 which was presented at the December 9 meeting of Ministers of Finance and Provincial Treasurers.

speechtext:

Does the Air Transport Committee, when granting licences to Canadian airlines, require them to integrate their schedules, where possible, with other airlines, so that passengers using more than one airline are not subject to long and unconscionable delays when transferring and, if not, has any consideration been given to instituting such a policy?
2.	For what reason is it necessary for Air Canada's Flight 135 to leave Montreal at 11.40, thus requiring passengers from the Atlantic Provinces arriving from EPA's Flight 101 and from Air Canada's Flight 639
Order Paper Questions
travelling to Ottawa to remain in Montreal until 15.15 hours from 11.30 hours and 11.50 hours respectively?

subsubtopic: AIR SERVICE SCHEDULES
speechtext:
1. Air
Transport Committee policy is reflected in the Air Carrier Regulations which by Section 18 (1) (f) requires licensed class 1, 2, 8 and 9-2 air carriers to provide reasonable through service to connect with other carriers, and by Section 86 requires such carriers to furnish copies of their schedules to connecting carriers and to provide evidence that this has been done by a notation to this effect on any filing advice sent to the committee with any schedule or pattern filing or amendment.
2. Air Canada's Flight 135 is primarily intended to provide service from Ottawa to Toronto and Regina and is scheduled one hour later than the airline would actually prefer, due to difficulties in obtaining an available aircraft at an earlier hour. To provide a connection from EPA's flight, it would be necessary to delay AC 135 for a further 50 minutes, resulting in both an unacceptable deterioration in this flight's schedule and the loss of a flight frequency later in the day. A morning service, with a 50-minute connection in Montreal, and a direct late afternoon service is provided every day between Moncton and Ottawa. These services are considered more than adequate to handle an estimated flow of 20 to 30 passengers daily. Air Canada co-operates with all regional carriers to effect the best possible integration of schedules whenever and wherever possible, provided that there is not a prohibitive deterioration of Air Canada's services, and inefficient use of equipment and resources, or unacceptable increased costs.

speechtext: A supplementary to the Minister of Transport. Notwithstanding the fact that government transportation policy affects the whole of the country, he knows as well as anyone else that western Canada and eastern Canada are particularly concerned. In the light of the CTC decision this morning would the hon. gentleman be prepared to approach the railways in an attempt to get a voluntary agreement to extend the freeze at least until the government announces its new transportation policy?

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF FREEZE UNTIL GOVERNMENT ANNOUNCES NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is at least the tenth time I am asked this question in the House. I have indicated to the House what kind of distortion that partial freeze created, because when we speak about price freeze, freight rates freeze, we must not forget that only 22 per cent of railway freight rates are affected. Other rates are not. Maritime transportation, trucking and air transportation are not affected. So, to present this policy as a general price freeze in Canada is to make misrepresentations. Mr. Speaker, it must not be forgotten that if, on the one hand, railway companies have promised to maintain certain rates to their 1972 level, on the other hand, those who use railways have never promised not to increase their prices. That means that some have enjoyed lower rates without letting the public benefit from them.
Therefore, it is not really a solution. As I said, we wanted to give an example which has not been followed. We merely remove the small partial freeze and try to find a policy which would help Canadians in general, instead of being used as a mere pretence to ask the kind of questions I have been asked this afternoon.

The House resumed, from Monday, January 27, 1975, consideration of the motion of Mr. Danson that Bill C-46, to amend the National Housing Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, January 27, when I called it ten o'clock I was speaking on this very important bill, C-46, and the portion that I was extremely interested in and discussing at that time was a log housing program for our remote areas of northern Manitoba and other remote areas of Canada.
I would like to clear up one misconception which some people may have about log housing. The type of log housing I have been contemplating, and discussing with my colleagues and people in the north, is not a small 12 foot by 14 foot log shack which sits on the ground. I am talking about a log building with properly squared logs sitting on a solid foundation. The material to build these log homes can be found adjacent to almost all isolated communities, at least in northern Manitoba.
My reason for promoting log housing, first, is that in many areas in remote Manitoba there is a very high unemployment rate, and in order to build log houses we do not have to go into an extensive training program because the majority of people in these remote communities are now adept and quite capable of building themselves a good, solid log house. Until just recently CMHC did not recognize log housing.
Until recently CMHC would not recognize log housing, although loans were not available for the construction of log homes. This policy has now changed, and CMHC loans for the building of log houses are available, provided the homes meet certain standards.
We should also promote the building of log houses in isolated parts of Canada because of the general shortage of homes. At present, in the community of Cross Lake, there is a shortage of homes. They lack about 30 homes in that community of approximately 2,300. The people of the community cannot do as others do, move to other towns close
January 29, 1975

by, or into an apartment block. Most homes in Cross Lake are single family dwellings, and the 30 families without roofs over their heads must double up, live with relatives, or with anyone who will take them.
We should also promote log housing in view of the high cost of transporting building materials to some isolated northern communities. To some of these places building materials must be transported between 280 and 350 miles by truck and tractor train. By the time some of these materials arrive at their destination they are nothing but piles of scrap. Four by eight pieces of buffalo board may end up as bits and pieces, yet the people of the north are supposed to build homes with such material. That is my main reason for promoting the building of log houses. They are more suitable for the remote areas of Canada.
I draw attention to log homes being shipped from B.C. Several such homes are located in some of our finest cities. I think, therefore, that it would be wise to encourage the building of log homes in the north. The building industry could also be encouraged to supply log homes to many other cities of Canada. We have plenty of timber in our country, and there is a great deal of unemployment in remote areas. The building of such houses could provide employment.
Let me refer to a problem encountered especially on Indian reserves. In the past housing on Indian reserves has been supplied practically free of charge. I believe the department has charged a nominal fee of $25 per home. In such a situation, however, the sense of ownership of the occupant is lacking, as the person in the home feels the home does not belong to him. After all, he has invested only $25 in it. Therefore he does not feels he owns it; whereas, if he had built the house for himself he would enjoy a sense of ownership. The sorts of buildings I am speaking of are small, generally, and sitting on the ground. Perhaps the government might consider granting CMHC loans to such people on reserves, perhaps at reduced rates. Many people in such communities earn a wage and would be prepared to contribute to the cost of a home.
I believe that people want to participate in the building of their own log homes, but they must have the means with which to live while their homes are being built. If we are to promote the building of log houses on reserves we must deal with Indian leaders and with the Department of Indian Affairs. The government must try to provide money for log houses in communities such as Cross Lake. The people there, although originally not in favour of log housing, have now said that they would like to build log homes because the sorts of homes presently being built do not stand up under conditions of current use. In the long run we would save money by building log homes, for the simple reason that it costs a great deal to keep the other sorts of homes now being built in northern communities in good repair. Repair bills are a substantial factor in the cost of present housing in the north.
Let me correct a misconception. People think that many of the house repairs on Indian reserves are necessary because of the way people living in those houses misuse them. Well, Mr. Speaker, 95 per cent of the people who live in such homes look after them. The difficulty, as I suggested last Monday, is that the houses in those communities are not designed for the types of heating and plumbing
National Housing Act
systems which are necessary but which are non-existent in most of these houses.
I shall lend my full support to Bill C-46 because housing is the backbone of our country. At present all communities in northern Manitoba face an acute housing shortage. The sooner we pass this bill and make money available for new homes, the better I will be pleased.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in opening the debate on this bill the minister said this about the government's proposed housing programs, as recorded at page 2622 of Hansard:
As social housing programs, they are intended to help substantial numbers of Canadian families either to buy their own homes or to rent suitable accommodation at a cost they can afford.
Later in his speech he said:
... let me emphasize that the first concern of this government is with the human dimension of housing, with our commitment to provide every Canadian with access to good housing in a safe and satisfying community environment, at a cost he can afford.
If this bill were to accomplish that, the members of my party would support it wholeheartedly. But this bill will do nothing of the sort. It has been criticized by organizations interested in a non-pecuniary way in housing. And, because the bill falls so short of meeting the objectives which the minister outlined when speaking on it, we intend to vote against it.
The Canadian Council on Social Development, an organization which brings together all government and private agencies interested in health and welfare matters, issued a press release on December 13 dealing with the minister's proposals, as embodied in the bill. In a pamphlet entitled, "New Federal Housing Thrusts Cause Poor to Suffer," the council says in part;
Urban Affairs Minister Barney Danson's recent announcement of federal subsidies to private lenders, under the assisted home ownership and rental entrepreneur programs, as well as Finance Minister John Turner's November 18 budget, reveal a new and lamentable shift in federal housing policy, according to Serge Carreau, of the Housing Committee of the Canadian Council on Social Development.
Mr. Carreau called on Canadians today to oppose this shift in federal housing policy which he termed a dangerous precedent and one which will primarily benefit relatively affluent families rather than those most in need ...
The specific proposal outlined by Mr. Danson December 11, contrary to his assertion, will primarily benefit, rather, affluent middle income families.
I could go on quoting but I think I have quoted enough to show what the Canadian Council on Social Development thinks of the bill introduced by the minister.
The bill highlights the fundamental problem of housing in this country. We have encouraged, through housing legislation and the housing programs of this and previous governments, the development of class conflicting housing. This involves conflict between those who have houses and those who have not. Some have been permitted, have been encouraged by attractive provisions in the National Housing Act, to buy houses, the mortgages on which are guaranteed. In short, the money put out by mortgage companies and banks has been backed by government guarantees. So, certain people have been able to buy houses by virtue of assistance provided by the taxpayer.

January 29, 1975
National Housing Act
The provisions of the National Housing Act do not permit people with low or middle incomes to purchase or rent houses. These people are not permitted to rent housing accommodation near those who are able to buy their own houses.
We have a situation where the federal and provincial governments are willing to provide money under various provisions of the National Housing Act to build public housing units. However, municipalities and communities are doing everything they can to block these housing units which are so desperately needed. Those who are better off do not want what they consider to be substandard housing built near them, nor do they wish to associate with those they consider to be economically and socially inferior. That condition has existed since the end of World War II. It exists at the present time, and will continue to exist if we pass this bill.
I suggest that the present National Housing Act be scrapped. What we require is a national housing policy which will provide needed housing for everyone, regardless of income. In particular it should be available to those who cannot afford to buy or rent housing. This should not be done by the building of public housing, or limited dividend housing units. People without adequate housing do not want to live in them, and those with adequate housing do not want these anywhere near them. In a speech which he made in Toronto on January 25, the minister said, and I quote:
Everyone favours low-cost public housing, for example, but nobody wants it built next door.
The minister is quite right. In fact people not only do not want it next door, but do not want it within two or three miles of them. We do not want more public housing units or limited dividend housing units. What we need is housing which people can buy or rent, regardless of their income. If they cannot afford it, they should be given rental supplements.
There is a very good system in the Scandinavian countries. Regardless of income, people live in the same type of housing accommodation, in close proximity. This is high quality housing. It is as good as that purchased by those who can afford to buy their own homes. These housing units are not built to last 20 years, after which time they will become slums or semi-slums, but to last 100 years. That is the kind of housing we need. It is the kind of housing that is built in other countries.
The minister may think I am exaggerating in my criticism of what has been done up until this time. So that the minister may know I am not saying this for purely partisan political reasons, I wish to quote from a study of low-income housing, made on behalf of this government under a former minister, by Professor Charney of Montreal. I wish to refer to some of his observations about projects which had been built supposedly to meet the needs of people in low income groups. This study was not made 50, 25 or ten years ago. In spite of a great deal of hesitation and reluctance on the part of the former minister, it was published in July, 1971.
This is what Professor Charney had to say about the Mulgrave Park housing project in Halifax:

The project was isolated from its surroundings: yet little allowance was made to develop community amenities, such as a day-care centre or recreation facilities. The manager of the project has made a request for facilities, as yet to be provided.
Mulgrave Park is perceived by both its tenants and the general populace as the worst example of public housing in Halifax today- clearly distinguishable even in the "north end" where almost all of the public housing has been built to date. It is a ghetto characterized by low-income welfare typical conditions with a high proportion of mother-led families, estimated at nearly 50 per cent of the families in the project, and a lack of basic amenities.
I quote from what Professor Charney had to say about the Le Domaine project:
Poor design and poor materials were accepted in the interests of rapid completion. For example, where heating is inefficient, tenants will turn warm kitchens into bedrooms. Externally, the repetition of a small number of designs, the cramping of too many apartments into a given areas, are obvious causes of dissatisfaction among tenants.
Only the builders seem to gain valuable experience from such projects, learning with tacit CMHC approval how to cut costs, and get away with it, thus realizing higher returns on their investments. With CMHC to bail them out, they need not be truly competitive, i.e., provide the kind of housing they are expected to.
I now quote one paragraph of what Professor Charney had to say about the Fabreville project:
The site of this project is singularly inappropriate for the needs and capabilities of low-income groups. Situated on residual land facing major traffic arteries, far from employment, shopping and public transportation, car ownership is mandatory for this site. Although there are plans to provide some community facilities on the site at a later date no such facilities exist now. All those in the family that do not have mobility are virtually trapped.
In connection with the Norshire Gardens in Edmonton, Professor Charney said:
While the developer turned down over 600 of 800 applicants for apartments, and claimed that a majority were "unable to qualify because their maximum income exceeded $5,660" ... he apparently saw no reason to break down these statistics further and give a precise figure of those in the $5,000 to $5,660 income range who were turned down on account of being "very, very heavily in debt" ... One can question whether the developer was really interested in renting to low-income families at all.
I could take the rest of the day to read into the record Professor Charney's assessment of projects built not too long ago supposedly to meet the needs of those with low incomes.
I have before me a study conducted by the Canadian Council on Social Development in 1971 entitled, "Where the $200 Million Went". It is a commentary on the 1970 CMHC innovative program sponsored by a former minister in charge of housing. I quote from page 18 of the report:
While the committee considers that housing innovation promises to make an important contribution to widening housing opportunities for low income Canadians, the $200 million program cannot be regarded as making any notable advance in this direction ...
In addition, the committee believes it should be clearly recognized that there are hundreds of thousands of families and old people whose incomes are too low to enable them to take advantage of most of the accommodation built under this program .. .
Lest any believe that low income housing should be cheap housing, the committee strongly affirms that the path to housing those now denied good accommodation by the market does not lie in reducing environmental standards. If anything, low income Canadians need better housing than those who have access to other amenities of life.
January 29, 1975

I wish the minister would pay some attention, if not to me, then to what I consider to be one of the most objective and highly respected organizations in this country. Last, they say:
All Canadians should be guaranteed the right to decent housing, whether they can afford it or not. To achieve this the federal government must mount a systematic effort to revolutionize housing production and distribution.
Has there been any revolutionary effort since 1970? Of course not. All we have seen is more of the same-a repetition of the measures which have proved so inadequate in the past. Today the minister proposes we should merely carry on in the same way.
In 1973, Michael Dennis, who headed the main study carried out by the government in connection with housing, appeared before the Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. He made a presentation which, if listened to and digested by all members, would, I feel sure, make us all ashamed, regardless of party, of what we have permitted to happen in the field of housing in this country.
Let me read a couple of paragraphs from the comments made by Professor Dennis, who is now the head of the housing program for the City of Toronto and a key aide to Mayor Crombie of Toronto. He said:
Existing federal programs have been severely criticized for their artificial segregation of households by income group. This is particularly so in the case of public housing. The proposed legislation does not take account of this problem and unintentionally exacerbates it.
He was talking about certain proposed legislation. Have we paid any attention to this question since 1973? The answer is, of course, no. Professor Dennis went on to say:
Equally important, the bill should be amended to permit the rental of units in low rental housing projects and public housing projects to middle income families. At present, a low rental housing project is defined as a project to be leased to families of low income or such other persons as the corporation, under agreement with the owner, may designate .... The NHA must be amended to allow public housing and non-profit landlords to serve households beyond the low income level while retaining their preferred interest rates, on condition that middle income tenants not obtain the advantage of those preferred rates.
Have we done that? Of course not. Some hon. members may think I have been making suggestions which are impracticable. The minister might believe that they cannot be carried out. He would be right if he said that programs of this kind have not been accomplished or even attempted in this country. However, I put it to him that there are alternatives to the patchwork crazy quilt of policies adopted by this and former governments, policies which have failed so markedly to meet the needs of Canadians in the middle and lower income brackets.
Even if we continue to treat people in the upper income levels as generously as we are doing, and those in the middle and lower income levels in as niggardly a way as we are doing, must we go on denying inadequate housing to those who cannot afford to buy or rent decent accommodation because their incomes are too low? Other countries have found methods of providing their citizens with housing as a matter of right regardless of their ability to pay, without putting up housing units of low quality.
The Scandinavian countries have no such programs as ours. They do not build public housing ghettos. They do
National Housing Act
not put up sub-standard limited dividend housing projects which in 20 years become slums. They build housing, both for private ownership and for rent, which is available to all their citizens, including those who are not able to pay. People who cannot pay the economic rent are assisted through a system of rent subsidies, and in this way people at all income levels are able to live, not only in the same block but in the same housing units.
I have before me a booklet entitled "Social Benefits" in Sweden. It is published by the Swedish Institute, which includes the Swedish Employers Confederation, the Confederation of Swedish Trade Unions, and the Swedish Central Organization of Salaried Employees. I refer the minister to the section on housing which is entitled "Rent Allowances to Families with Children", and I wish to put on record a few paragraphs from this booklet because they show so clearly what is done in Sweden. The program followed in Sweden is one which is very much like the programs instituted in Denmark, Finland, Norway and the Federal Republic of Germany. I quote as follows:
State rent allowances are payable to families with at least one child which is wholly or partly maintained by the family at home. Taxable income... determines the amount of the allowance. The taxable incomes of both parents are aggregated unless they live apart. A family as defined for this purpose is a married couple with at least one child, or a single person with at least one child. Unmarried couples living together are classed as married if they were previously married to each other or if they have or have had children by each other.
The rent allowance is 75 kr per month per child if the breadwinners' taxable income assessed for national income tax does not exceed 21,000 kr. If the taxable income is higher, the rent allowance is reduced by 12 per cent of taxable income between 21,000 and 26,000 kr, by 18 per cent of taxable income between 26,000 and 36,000 kr, and by 24 per cent of taxable income over 36,000 kr. If the family joint property is worth more than 50,000 kr, one-fifth of the excess above that figure is added to the taxable income.
I interrupt my quoting to tell the minister that a kroner is worth about 25 cents. So we are talking about people who have a taxable income of $5,000 and upward. In addition to rent subsidies there are municipal rent allowances. Let me put on record what they are.
Municipal rent allowances are paid by most local authorities and are intended for families with children paying high rents or heavy mortgage costs. To qualify for this allowance the family must have title to and occupy a dwelling. The cost of occupancy must be at least 425 kr a month.
That is just over $100 a month.
The allowable cost of occupancy is reduced if the family has a lodger or occupies an unnecessarily large dwelling. The income limits for Municipal Rent Allowances are higher than for the State Allowance. Depending on the number of children and the amount of the rent, the allowance is usually between 20 and 420 kr per month.
That is from $5 to over $100 per month.
Municipal rent allowances are payable in respect of children under 17.
And so on. On the same page in this pamphlet there is a table which is too detailed for me to read, but let me give an example, for the benefit of the minister, of the state and municipal rent allowance paid in Sweden.
For a family of five-husband, wife and three children- which has an income of between 21,000 kroner and 36,600 kroner a year-roughly $5,000 to $9,500 a year-the monthly rent is between 425 kroner to 800 kroner a month, or

January 29, 1975
National Housing Act
between $100 a month and about $200 a month. The rent supplement, state and municipal, can vary from a minimum of 10 kroner per month, about $2.50, to 545 kroner a month, roughly $125. Because of this type of program, people in Sweden do not have public housing units, limited dividend housing, or assisted home ownership programs. Yet everyone in Sweden has adequate accommodation.
I have a lot of respect for the minister and I believe he wants to do a job and meet the needs of the Canadian people for adequate housing. I also believe he knows that the housing needs of hundreds of thousands of Canadians have not been met, certainly not in any kind of adequate manner.
I urge the minister to free himself from the too close embraces that housing ministers usually get from the senior officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the building industry, bank and mortgage companies and others, who until now have given housing ministers advice that has been poor and inadequate, and that has led to programs which have obviously failed to meet the housing needs of the Canadian people.
I urge the minister to travel away from Ottawa and meet people who live in poor housing. If necessary, he should visit countries that have demonstrated that they have answers to the housing needs of their own people. Let him vsit the Scandinavian countries and the Federal Republic of Germany, which I and some other members of parliament visited last December. He will not see any slums in their cities. Nor will he see any gerry-building or low quality public housing which looks, and is, substandard.
If the minister would do this I am sure he would be able to develop programs that meet the housing needs of the people of this country, programs that would not be the disgrace that up to now has been the case. Then he will begin to give people in Canada, and especially people of low income, the same kind of decent housing other Canadians have been able to get, housing of which all Canadians can be proud. If the minister will do this he will do a job for the people of this country which housing ministers until now certainly have been unable to do.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was disappointed to learn that some opposition members who have spoken on Bill C-46 seem to have misunderstood the spirit and the significance of the proposed amendments to the National Housing Act. Mr. Speaker, I should like to place this bill in its context as part of the housing policy of the federal government.
Most criticisms passed on Bill C-46 are undoubtedly due to a misunderstanding. These amendments are said to be the only way the government has found to solve the housing problem in Canada. In fact, they are the extension of a vast range of existing programs which have greatly benefited Canadians.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext: That is your only answer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious from the remarks made by some members of the opposition that they have missed the point. They have forgotten the wide spectrum of measures we have already brought before the Canadian people. No one has mentioned the very exhaustive measures contained in the present government's policy of social housing. I could go through the list. There is the Assisted Home Ownership Program from which
30,000	families benefited last year. Under the bill now before the House this program will be extended to those who obtain loans from private sources and who conform to other conditions.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext: How many people in your constituency will be able to benefit?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Let me tell the hon. member that yesterday I was in Saskatchewan. A family on welfare with an annual income of less than $6,000 a year can buy a single dwelling unit costing $25,000 with the help of AHOP and a $1,000 grant from the province of Saskatchewan. So even a family on welfare, with the help of AHOP and the provincial government of Saskatchewan, can own a single housing unit costing $25,000! This is the lowest level, and the range of income extends to $16,000 or $17,000 elsewhere in the country.
I have spoken so far only of AHOP, and I should now like to detail the other measures. There is rental housing assistance under which we grant a loan of 100 per cent to non-profit organizations, church service groups, at 10 per cent forgiveable. I know it hurts the hon. member to learn of all these programs because obviously he is not aware of them. In addition, there is privately funded rental housing, as set out in the bill, co-operative housing assistance-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext:
When I have finished my speech the hon. member can make another speech. We have public housing assistance, home improvement loans, land assembly assistance, the new communities bank, serviced land, land banking-and I could go on and on. If hon. members want to criticize some of the measures in this bill, let them put them in perspective and not forget all of the programs we have put together during the last few years.
I do not for a moment wish to minimize the housing problems which we will be facing in the years ahead. At the same time I would remind the House that in the six years since 1969 well over one million homes have been built in Canada, surpassing by a comfortable margin the requirements set out by the Economic Council of Canada prior to that time. This was achieved in large measure as a result of federal policies and programs put into effect by CMHC.
We realize that good housing is fundamental to a sound and healthy society, and we have designed programs that are realistic enough to meet the current needs of Canadians and lead to continued long-term stability.
The substantial drop in housing starts last year from the record level of 1973 was due, as hon. members know, to a number of factors that are by no means unique to the
January 29, 1975

Canadian scene. The worldwide problem of inflation, unusually high interest rates and shortage of mortgage funds, which was one of the major reasons, and other factors combined to produce a shortage of reasonably priced housing and, in particular, a serious shortage of housing that low and moderate income families could afford. That situation was aggravated by the inflation psychosis and rising and somewhat unrealistic expectations about the standard of living which could be sustained by our rate of economic growth.
In putting the proposed amendments into context it is useful to remember that, although housing starts were down last year, actual completions reached the record high of 257,243 units, well above the requirements of the population growth and family formations, and by far the largest number of units ever completed in a single year. I am not speaking here just of starts, but of houses built and ready to be occupied and lived in, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I point out to the House that the actual difficulty did not lie with the housing supply, but actually with the cost of housing. That is why the government's action principles and programs aim at a certain number of objectives. Most of all, we want to help families that cannot cope with the high cost of their accommodation. We urge builders to redirect their production to the gamut of low and moderately-priced housing, whether for sale or rental. Through our help and incentives, we urge municipalities to service a greater number of building lots, and we use our resources to channel new capital into the housing market.
We trust that, thanks to those action principles, our main housing needs shall be met this year.

I should like to remind hon. members of the relevant CMHC programs and their effects, and point out the importance of the proposed new legislation in providing homes for Canadians.
The Assistance to Home Ownership Program, introduced in July, 1973, was designed to help low and moderate income families with at least one child to own homes without spending more than a reasonable proportion of their incomes on mortgage payments and municipal taxes. Through low interest loans and interest reducing grants some 20,000 families last year bought homes from Central Mortgage and Housing. The bulk of the purchasers were families with incomes of $10,000 or less.
In some parts of the country it served families with incomes as low as $4,000. That means that people with an annual income of $4,000, many on social welfare, were able, through that program, to buy houses! They received two forms of assistance-one a direct subsidy to help them pay the loan, and the other to reduce the interest rates.
Although at first it was possible to buy existing housing through AHOP, it soon became apparent that new housing must be built to add to the existing stock, while increasing employment opportunities in the building industry, and during the late stages of the program last year AHOP assistance was confined to new housing only. It is obviously still essential that new housing be built, and for that reason the AHOP program, including the proposed pri-
National Housing Act
vately funded AHOP, will continue to restrict purchasing to new homes.
Let me emphasize here that the amendments are designed to expand the AHOP program beyond its present limits by attracting private capital. In other words, under these provisions of the bill, the interest reducing feature, grants would be paid to people who get private loans from approved lenders to buy homes as long as they qualify under the general terms and conditions of the AHOP program and are first time purchasers of new homes. The grants may be as much as $600 a year.
The regular AHOP will continue in effect, as the minister explained when introducing the legislation, and will continue to benefit low income families as before.
There is a misconception, particularly by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), that only high income families qualify for AHOP assistance. He makes the extraordinary suggestion that AHOP in Toronto and Vancouver will serve only families making $19,000 or more. The fact is that in these cities government AHOP and private AHOP together will serve a range of families with incomes as low as $11,000 and up to $17,500. People with incomes of $19,000 are obviously not included.
Despite the very emphatic statements made by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson), some hon. members opposite persist in implying that the assisted rental provisions of the bill are for the benefit of builders and owners. There is an urgent need for construction of rental accommodation at prices people of modest means can afford. The purpose of the amendment is precisely that, to create rental housing at moderate rates, and builders will be bound in agreements with CMHC to see that federal contributions are passed on to the tenants.
By obtaining loans at the preferred rate of 8 per cent from CMHC a landlord will be able to have his rents reduced accordingly. Of course he cannot obtain that preferred loan interest rate of 8 per cent unless he enters into an agreement, assuring that his rents are going to be fair and reasonable.
As the minister mentioned, these two measures will provide about $1 billion in mortgages for Canadians, particularly those in urban areas, to obtain accommodation at affordable prices. It is estimated that the two programs and CMHC direct lending will provide 28,000 units of accommodation for our wage earners which otherwise would not have been built in 1975.
It is evident that the current housing situation demands quick starts on construction, and the thrust of the amendments is to encourage builders, as well as municipalities, to think in terms of immediate, not delayed action.
During the debate on this bill reference has been made to the very real plight of low income families, as if all the social benefits of the National Housing Act had suddenly been repealed and were no longer in effect. Let me again set the record straight. The foundation of this government's housing policy has always been the provision of good housing at affordable costs for all Canadians, with particular concern for those Canadians who are in need of help. This is particularly true today in our present economic conditions.

January 29, 1975
National Housing Act
I might point out that since 1969 we have produced well over a quarter of a million housing units for low income people at a total investment of more than $2.5 billion dollars. This amounts to more than three times the total number built in the preceding 22 years since the National Housing Act came into effect. So, since 1969 we have spent over $2.5 billion for low and moderate income people in the last 6 years.

But figures tell only part of the story. The government's principles state that the people must have the widest possible range of choices as to their kind of accommodation and the type of use. We have long since moved away from the Shanty Town concept, where tenants were massed in public housing or government assisted buildings in downtown areas.
Our housing programs have allowed numerous low-income families to get their own housing. Others could rent comfortably at moderate, subsidized prices. The land-lease feature afforded non-profit housing projects by the proposed legislation is part of a permanent policy of efficiently helping the low-income group and retired people. [English]	0
The government, through CMHC, has proceeded on a number of other fronts to assist Canadians-particularly those of moderate means-to have good housing in a satisfactory environment.
The Neighbourhood Improvement Program, for example, is conserving and improving neighbourhoods in danger of decay and destruction. Within these areas the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program is helping home owners to repair and restore their dwellings to an acceptable standard of health and safety.
We are confident we will achieve 210,000 housing starts this year.

We are not being pessimistic but we do not hope to reach the record level of last year which was over 260,000 units. This year, due to the provisions in this bill and the incentive for private funds to be channelled to the housing industry, we hope to achieve over 210,000 units.
We do not pretend that there are easy answers to the problem of giving all Canadians access to good housing at affordable prices, and that challenge becomes doubly difficult in the present circumstances. But by implementing realistic and effective legislative, fiscal and other measures we are making, and will continue to make, significant headway. In the meantime it should not be forgotten, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians continue to benefit from some of the most comprehensive and humane housing laws in the world.
