subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments to make on Bill C-46. I do not intend to repeat some of the criticisms of my colleagues which they made in a meaningful and objective way with regard to some inequities in the bill, but I hope to be able to refer to some of the comments made by the hon. member for Matane (Mr. De Bane).
Certainly, as the minister mentioned, going back to history to put the matter into perspective, there have been countless programs-and I know of them because many have been applied in my district-introduced by successive governments. Many millions of dollars have been poured into housing in Canada, and certainly many thousands of Canadians have derived some good as a result. I think everybody agrees that the minister, since taking on the portfolio is making a determined effort to do his job, and I think he will listen to sound advice from members of the opposition who have a particular interest in housing in the interests of the parts of the country they represent.
When one looks at the various programs available under CMHC, together with the provincial programs, one cannot but agree that there should be no Canadian without shel-
January 29, 1975

ter. I refer to programs to provide shelter for persons with an income of $3,000, programs sponsored by the provinces.
We hear the often repeated cliche, again referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), that no Canadian should be denied a home, regardless of his income or where he lives. But for some reason, in spite of the great number of programs, there are many Canadians who have difficulty acquiring accommodation because of the bureaucratic entanglements, and because of the need for consultation with the various provinces as well as the existence of various municipal bylaws. I hope that in this regard the minister will make a sincere attempt, in discussions with CMHC, to untangle that bureaucratic mess and the red tape which one has to go through in applying for a loan, which is most frustrating.
If I may refer to the Assisted Home Ownership Program I am pleased, as others are, to note that more funding will be directed to this area. I was disappointed, however, that the minister made no mention of re-introducing the availability of funds for the purchase of existing homes, and also of removing the restriction against young, newly married couples who cannot qualify for a loan under the Assisted Home Ownership Program unless they have a child. This is absolutely amazing to me. It is obviously contradictory of other government policies-for example I will mention family planning. To my mind such a restriction is discriminatory.
We all know that there are many young couples who, when planning their future, want first to acquire a home before starting to raise a family. This opportunity should not be denied them, particularly when they cannot afford to borrow through other sources or under other programs.
I was also disappointed that there are no provisions in the bill to provide more funding for, nor is anything contained in the bill with regard to the Neighbourhood Improvement Program and the Residential Rehabilitation Program which the parliamentary secretary mentioned. This has been in existence for over a year, and it is obvious that, as usual, it only applies to large urban centres. 1 am sure the minister will be quick to recall that in my province two of the larger centres have already received loans and grants under NIP, in the region of $1 million. This amount will barely scratch the surface when taking the need into account.
The rehabilitation factor under the Neighbourhood Improvement Program, which should be directed on a massive basis, would overcome the needs of many thousands of Canadians in the lower and middle income level. Under the rehabilitation section of the program those earning $6,000 or less can borrow up to $5,000 to improve their homes, and have to pay only half of it back, with a reduced scale of relief to those earning up to $11,000.
This is a good program, but in Newfoundland, after 15 months, I think the amount of $600,000 had been paid in grants, and that did not go very far.
Later on, I will quote some statistics.
When this program was announced last year I was overjoyed because of the many advantages that I saw in it, which allow the home owner to bring his home up to a
National Housing Act
better standard and give it longer life, besides enabling the owner to put in proper wiring, heating and, more particularly, insulation. If we were to look at this program just from the point of view of saving fuel, which is such a crisis in Canada, just imagine how many hundreds of thousands of homes are not properly insulated, and the added fuel cost to the low income earner, those on fixed incomes and pensioners. Their fuel costs are so much higher in the cold winters due to improper insulation.
How many homes are being destroyed by fire each year because of faulty wiring, or because homes in rural communities have to rely on oil stoves rather than having furnaces, which could be installed under this program? Statistics are available to show that countless thousands of homes across Canada fall into this category. Yet the government has taken so long to reach an agreement with the provinces on the areas to be designated, and here we are with another winter upon us with little action being directed towards implementing those programs.
If the government in its thrust for conservation wants to conserve fuel, more effort to implement this rehabilitation program on a massive scale should be undertaken immediately. The same applies to the doddling and blundering going on in relation to rural housing programs where supposedly, on paper, rehabilitation grants can be extended to the rural areas of our country which cannot qualify under the Neighbourhood Improvement Program.
The long drawn out consultative process denies many poor Canadians the advantages of these programs. There is a need for occupational standards to be set up, and areas of special help to be designated by the provinces; and still people wait for the benefits which could be made available thus saving many hundreds of millions of dollars for the country. I have been trying since these programs were established at all levels to get more emphasis placed on them, particularly in my province of Newfoundland, but all that I get is the type of letter which I received just this past September from the president of CMHC. He always ends his letters by saying that:
I share your concern that we see tangible benefits from these programs for low and moderate income Canadians at the earliest opportunity and you may be assured that CMHC is doing its utmost in this regard.
I cannot tell this to my people because they would think it is my answer to their problem.
I was looking at some census statistics recently from my province because of my particular concern for housing in that province. Those statistics emphasize the particular difficulties for prospective home owners. I will relate some of the statistics on incomes as tabulated in 1971.
We have a population of 532,000; 118,000 of those people are earning less than $3,000 a year; 57,000 are earning between $3,000 and $6,000; another 33,000 are earning between $6,000 and $10,000. So there are not too many who qualify under any of the programs, and the programs should be extended further to the people who need them. I must admit that these are not all prospective home buyers. Since 1971 I am sure that there has been an improvement, because there is a new Progressive Conservative government in Newfoundland. These statistics certainly serve to indicate that more effort must be extended towards all

January 29, 1975
National Housing Act
areas of that province, and I would like to mention some of these for the minister's attention.
I wonder why more effort is not directed toward home improvement loans, and why the government is not taking the initiative in this respect. If section 28, which applies in this case, had been extended the government could have achieved the same purpose and avoided a long drawn out process without encroaching on provincial jurisdictions.
Under section 28 loans are made available for financing of improvements to existing housing, multiple family units, even buildings consisting of business premises and family dwellings, with $4,000 loans available to cover the cost of labour, materials, repairs, home additions and almost every purpose. It is a wonderful program. I hope that the minister will use these millions of dollars to extend this program so that those Canadians mentioned earlier can have the advantage of bringing their homes up to a decent standard for a longer life, and help reduce the number of these people who must try to build new homes because they cannot repair their own, or because they are not worth repairing.
This home improvement loan program is another excellent program, and all the minister has to do is to amend the section to insert the forgiveness factor. Then the people could apply directly to CMHC rather than having to go through the long process in waiting for provincial governments to designate areas. As most hon. members have indicated, I am sure we all agree in principle with Bill C-46, particularly where efforts will be made to employ more capital for funding assisted home ownership and to allow CMHC to acquire leased land for non-profit housing.
A great need in most provinces, and particularly mine, is the provision of sewage treatment systems, and I am glad to see that the minister is expanding aid to that area, which indeed should be a top priority item for every community in Canada. I think every community, regardless of its size, must have a proper, basic water and sewage system, not only for housing development but also from a health aspect.
More attention must be paid in my province to the acquiring of land. I understand from statistics that the average cost of a building lot in Newfoundland is around $7,000. These figures must be old, because I understand it is now closer to $10,000. So, how are these people, in the income brackets I referred to, even to acquire a piece of land on which to build a home?
I hear that $10 million is to be spent in Corner Brook on a regional college. Next year 500 students will come in, some with families, and 150 teachers with families. There has been no effort, other than that made by the municipality, to provide homes for them. I am told that lots will sell for not less than $10,000. What are these people to do? The solution to the problem might be limited dividend housing.
I hope the minister realizes the need and, when he meets with the minister responsible for municipal affairs and housing in the province, probably this week, I hope he will bring this problem to his attention.
Referring to the public housing sector the parliamentary secretary spoke about the person getting $3,000 a year and

being able to qualify for assistance under the Assisted Home Ownership Program. That is fine. But how can we provide public housing in Newfoundland when the lowest tender for row housing given to the province ran at $45,000 per unit? There is a firm in Newfoundland which can provide a three-bedroom pre-fabricated house for $18,000, and a four-bedroom pre-fabricated house for $23,000. I hope this builder can get together with the minister. I hope something will come of that meeting.
Instead of building houses which will cost at least $45,000 per unit-which is ridiculous-why does the government not consider providing, say, the basement and land, the costs of which would go a long way toward the cost of a home, and allow people 15, 25 or 35 years to pay? We could provide pre-fabricated houses on an emergency basis, and so relieve much of the pressure.
Let me deal with veterans' housing. The parliamentary secretary referred to some of our housing programs. I am aware of all the co-op housing programs, non-profit housing programs, and residential and rehabilitation programs, as well as the NIP programs, RAP, and most of the others. He talked about the thrust of public housing. Let me say that we shall see more of a thrust in that direction. In two cities of my riding there are upwards of 1,000 people on the waiting list for housing. They have been given top priority. The housing situation has been reported as ridiculous. The Corner Brook Housing Corporation and other housing corporations realize that they cannot do anything dramatic when one apartment becomes available in the public housing sector.
Let me tell the parliamentary secretary about what happens in rural communities. In one case, according to the survey done by the provincial command of the Canadian Legion, which was given $38,000 to do a housing survey, a double amputee, a man lacking both his legs, has to be carried out every day to the outhouse. Of course he must go there if he is to function properly. This type of thing is embarrassing to mention. All the same if things are improving, they are improving too slowly.
If I may dwell on veterans' housing, we are all aware that the Veterans Land Act will be phased out in two months. The minister promised that the government will come up with a new and improved veterans' housing program. I hope he is right, Mr. Speaker, because the need is there, even though the department does not agree and figures that the Veterans Land Act has outlived its usefulness. I am awaiting answers from the director of the veterans land administration, to find out how many applications have been made since we forced the government to extend the act at least for one year.
Still not many hundreds of veterans remain to be dealt with, and they have sent letters to support their requests for help. These people require homes and should be given the advantage of the Veterans Land Act for as long as they live. Since the government does not agree to extend the act, I am getting a bit suspicious about the promises of the minister. I know discussions may be going on, but I hope he is not just waiting out the few months before the act is phased out. I hope he will not then say he can do nothing. We shall see. I hope that the minister, and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs who will be directly concerned about veterans' housing, will come up with a program to
January 29, 1975

help veterans. Let us do this under Bill C-46, so that veterans who may be denied an opportunity to own housing because of the phasing out of the Veterans Land Act will not feel so badly.
I have mentioned many of the problems of the people of Newfoundland. Probably I have been parochial. What I said applies to people all over Canada, and to many in rural Canada. As I said, I am sure the minister will do all he can to improve housing conditions in this country. He can rest assured that he will have the support of the opposition, and the advice of the opposition. I hope he will co-operate with us, so that we can come up with a proper housing program for Canadians.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we have before us a bill which, on the surface, appears to be a step, however small, in the right direction to help the average working Canadian obtain a home at reasonable cost. We have heard statements in this debate about this objective. It is not new. What we heard from the minister was not a new statement on policy or principle. Unfortunately we have failed to move far in the direction in which we hope to make considerable progress in future.
We in my party have been greatly disturbed by the cavalier attitude of the government in the last two or three years. We do not care for the attitude it has shown to the housing crisis of Canada. On November 18, 1974, as recorded at page 1426 of Hansard, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) said in his budget statement about measures to stimulate residential construction:
The projected weakness in this sector of our economy troubles me a good deal. It threatens to reduce employment, raise production costs and increase prices and rents.
I am sure all Canadians were tremendously relieved to hear that the minister was finally troubled about the housing situation in the country. We in the opposition have been warning the minister for well over one year about prospects for the housing situation in Canada. He was warned repeatedly in the days of the minority twenty-ninth parliament, both by my leader and by the former leader of the NDP. He was warned by a great many members of the House that Canada was facing an unprecedented rise in interest rates, land costs and house prices. So, after all this time, after interest rates have risen to their highest level in history, some 14 per cent, after land costs have spiralled to completely ridiculous levels and house prices have sky-rocketed to unprecedented levels, the minister has finally said he is troubled.
I am sure that this is great consolation to the Canadian taxpayers who must pay 14 per cent in interest, pay $30,000 for a building lot, and $55,000 for a house which one and a half years ago would have cost about $23,000.
I am sure they are tremendously relieved and re-assured to know that the Minister of Finance was troubled a good deal. Let me ask: where was he when we needed him? Where was the Minister of Finance when the people of Canada needed him to deal with this particular problem? The government of Canada has a tremendous responsibility in encouraging the provision of houses for the people of this nation.
National Housing Act
Today we heard an outline of some of the programs. The parliamentary secretary took some pride in the fact there was such a multiplicity of plans. However, with the plans provided we should have made far greater progress in the provision of adequate homes for Canadians than has been made up to the present time.
We are faced with the situation where housing starts in Canada have fallen off drastically. The government must introduce new measures to stimulate growth in this very important sector of the economy. This present measure should have been introduced last August or September when the market was obviously in a decline. However, that is not the practice of this government.
As the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) often says, the government is like a doctor trying to treat a patient who is bleeding to death by applying a bandaid. When will the government learn that answers to critical problems in our economy are not found in bandaid approaches, but in comprehensive, rational policies that are designed to meet specific problems and needs? These should not be applied after the fact as the present government has so often done.
In the first week of October last year the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) asked the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) about the sharp decline in housing starts between August, 1973, and August, 1974. What was the minister's response? I quote from page 28 of Hansard:
Well, Mr. Speaker, I suggest there is not a housing crisis in this country.
That was a rather remarkable retort. I do not know what the Minister of State for Urban Affairs calls a crisis, but I do know that about one and a half months later the situation had deteriorated even more so, so much more that his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), stood in this chamber and said he was troubled about it.
I wish to touch briefly on some of the elements that appear to make up the government's approach to the serious problem of housing. I do not wish to repeat all that has been said about the Registered Home Ownership Plan since May 1974, the time its provisions were introduced. However, I do wish to ask how many young Canadians with average incomes can save $100 a year, let alone $1,000 a year for ten years? I submit that anyone with such an income as to be able to save $1,000 a year can go all the way, and immediately make a down-payment on a house. He would have a high enough income to do so.
In ten years, which is the maximum number of years for participation in this plan, how far does the minister think $10,000 will go toward buying a house? The way housing prices have been increasing since the Minister of Finance took over that portfolio, $10,000 will not go very far. Also, should we ask our young people to wait ten years before buying their own home? I submit we should not ask them to do that. Let me just say I am quite skeptical about the program.
Last November the Minister of Finance introduced a measure to eliminate part of the tax on building materials. He said at that time, and I quote:
It has been a subject matter of debate in this House.

January 29, 1975
National Housing Act
True enough, it has been, but thanks only to the members of the opposition parties, the party to which I belong in particular. Over the past number of years we have constantly raised this matter for debate. The government would have been happy just to forget about it, but this is one area where persistence has at least had half a result. I suppose the old adage is still true that half a loaf is better than no loaf at all. However, I cannot understand why this penny pinching attitude has been adopted and pursued. Is the minister too proud to make an about-face and adopt the total proposal we have made? I hope not.
The Minister of Finance was not too proud when he wholeheartedly adopted my leader's proposal for indexing personal incomes two years ago. As my leader said at that time, the Minister of Finance swallowed himself. Perhaps he should swallow himself again and not just reduce the sales tax on building materials by 50 per cent. Many members, including myself, made this point in the debate on the excise tax bill. I will not pursue it further.
Another element in the government's approach to housing has been to request principal lenders to loan money for homes of all prices rather than just lower and middle-priced housing. Does the minister understand what is going on today?
A home at $40,000 may be low priced compared to a home at $98,000, but for the average Canadian who has to pay $30,000 for a building lot with a mortgage at 12 to 14 per cent, with monthly payments on principal, interest and taxes of $350 to $400, a home is as out of reach at $40,000 as it is at $98,000. That all begs the question really, because in the major population centres in this country there just are not homes people can buy for even $40,000.
Perhaps one can buy condominiums or other housing for $40,000 in the urban centres, but I fail to see how the minister's proposal to have money loaned for higher-priced accommodation will help the condominium market. That market has apparently been eligible for loans all along. The minister considers $40,000 to be low-priced accommodation. In any case this proposal is completely fatuous.
The much touted piece of political puffery, as my colleague the hon. member for Calgary North calls the $500 grant to people buying new moderately-priced housing units for the first time, is hardly worth talking about. It is a small step in the right direction, but fails sadly to meet the needs of the present time. The restrictions are so many and so varied that this is pretty well ruled out as an adequate answer to the housing problem. For example, it must be the first home, a new home, and of limited value.
A few days ago I received a packet of cartoons from someone in my constituency. I do not know who sent them. One in particular caught my attention. It showed a man talking about how governments are trying to help the little people. He said "I know they are always talking about doing something to help the little people, but my problem is I am never little enough to qualify." That is true in many instances. These programs do not, and will not meet the needs of the average Canadian with regard to housing.
I really do not understand why the government did not go all the way. I submit the government will have to take

considerably more action than it is prepared to take through this bill to accomplish the aims it has outlined as its objectives. As I said at the outset, the $600 a year subsidy is a good proposal as far as it goes. But we would prefer to see the amount of the subsidy equal, or nearly equal, to the amount the low or middle income person pays in interest on residential mortgages during the year. We can only hope that the small step being taken in the proposal before us will be followed in the not-too-distant future by a longer step.
If the minister really wishes to get our housing industry moving in order to construct the dwellings we need, and if he really wants to help Canadians purchase their own homes, he would listen to the proposals put forward by my party, suggestions we have been making over the last number of years. I would refresh the hon. gentleman's memory by recounting some of them for him. First, as I have indicated, we favour the elimination of all of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials for use in residential construction-not just 6 per cent of the tax, but all of it. Provision should be made at the same time for a rollback in price amounting to 11 per cent in order to ensure that the consumer should benefit.
Second, our party favours an allowance of a percentage of interest payments on residential mortgages being deductible from personal income tax. This could be done, if necessary, on a graduated scale to ensure that lower income families would benefit as much as middle-income families. The amount paid in municipal taxes, or some portion thereof, should also be made tax deductible.
Third, we would encourage the financial institutions of this country to make mortgage money available at more reasonable interest rates. Ten per cent is too high. All that is necessary is a rate one half of one per cent higher than the Bank of Canada rate; CMHC, which would be responsible to our minister in charge of housing, would be encouraged to lend at more reasonable rates of interest.
Fourth, we would take the necessary steps to ensure the collection of serviced land for housing. We would not hide behind the constitution, as the government has done in some instances. I realise that many of these proposals would require consultation with provincial governments, but it seems to me we could arrive at a more reasonable interpretation of our constitution-that it could be used, not to keep Canadians in difficult situations but as a liberating instrument to benefit all our citizens.
The measure before us today is certainly a step in the right direction, but the government must be more imaginative in its approach; it must move more rapidly and more decisively if the housing needs of the country are to be met, and if citizens in all income categories are to enjoy accommodation adequate to their needs.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I believe the minister is, or should be, as concerned as we all are-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext: He is right here, over on this side.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext:
It is better to have him on my right than on my left. I assume he is as concerned as we all are about the
January 29, 1975

housing situation. Housing costs have reached the limit. Land costs are out of this world. The total cost of housing, whether owned or rented, is out of line altogether. In addition the slump in the housing industry has created a good deal of unemployment, not only in my own constituency but in a large number of other constituencies across the land, with resulting ill-effects on all aspects of the economy. The situation is serious. With all respect to the minister, I believe he has crept away, or walked away, or run away from this situation. This is a crisis, and apparently it is one which the government is unwilling to face.
I have been concerned with housing for many years at the municipal level, and I am not convinced that all possible steps have been taken to provide decent housing for all our citizens. The real difficulty underlying the situation stems from the government's failure to wrestle inflation to the ground, in the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) phrase, to reduce high interest rates and to cut down wasteful government expenditure. If interest charges were reduced, monthly payments would be lower. If construction costs were reduced the burden on home owners would be less. If government waste in connection with unnecessary and luxurious programs were eliminated, more money could be provided to those who cannot afford to satisfy their reasonable housing needs.
Public housing schemes are of great importance, not only for senior citizens and families in need but for adults in need of this type of accommodation. The CMHC must take the bull by the horns and cut out the red tape, dispense with unnecessary studies, consultations and consultants' fees. It must question the need to make up to 10 copies of every item. It must cut down the bureaucracy which scares the ordinary young couple away. Like many Crown agencies CMHC has become the victim of an overrated, over-populated bureaucracy, a great deal of its budget being spent on administration instead of on housing.
In my own constituency there is an acute need for housing and I urge the CMHC to continue its efforts, but in a new direction so as to make it easier to obtain financial assistance for the purchase of homes. It is true the minister is proposing some changes in the act, but I suggest these are not changes which will make it easy for young persons or senior citizens to find suitable housing.
There is another matter which puzzles me in this connection, and I am afraid I shall be chastized by members of my own profession for raising it now. A purchaser who buys through CMHC is not permitted to choose his own lawyer or solicitor but is bound to retain the solicitor to whom he has been referred by the Corporation.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext: They might choose somebody who was not a Liberal. God forbid!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I don't know. Obviously they are chosen from a list made up by the government. Yet of all the things a person purchases, his home is probably the most important, and surely in this connection he should be able to get independent advice from someone employed by him, not advice from someone chosen by a government or a Crown agency from a list prepared by the government, or by an association on behalf of the government.
National Housing Act
If this practice continues, then at least the solicitor who does the work should be asked to do it on a charitable basis. When an individual is purchasing a property he should be able to retain his own solicitor.
I should also like to ask the minister whether he is prepared to amend the bill to provide financing for mobile homes. At the present time financing for mobile homes is done by financial institutions which charge anywhere from 18 to 23 per cent, and there is no way a young person, or indeed anybody, can afford that rate.
I should like the minister to answer my questions when he closes the debate. I would also like to know why CMHC continues to pass the buck, sometimes to the provinces, sometimes to the municipalities, sometimes to church clubs and organizations, as well as service clubs, in regard to assisting public housing, and in particular senior citizens' housing. I suggest it is time that the minister and CMHC got down to the grass roots level, rather than stand on his pedestal here in Ottawa, with his big building on one of the Ottawa streets. Doing this will not solve the housing problem in places like Vancouver, Toronto, Moncton, Halifax and St. John's.
The government must be prepared to shoulder the load of financial assistance not only for senior citizens' housing complexes but also for geriatric care; the two cannot be separated. To accomplish this a program must be followed that will embrace the entire spectrum of housing and care for senior citizens. Although much has been done, much more remains to be done. Let the minister not sit upon his so-called laurels; the government must do better to assist those who need housing.
I suggest the minister and his department deal directly with communities and with public housing projects. We always hear the excuse that under the BNA Act the provinces must be consulted. I suggest that the act has been circumvented before, and can be circumvented again. We are facing a housing crisis such that we can no longer tolerate any delay. Now is the time to cut out waste, and for CMHC and the department to do their homework. We must eliminate politics and patronage, and expedite housing construction, free from red tape, political interference and delay in provincial consultation.
As a further incentive to home ownership, real estate taxes and interest rates on mortgages should be deductible for income tax purposes. This is the case elsewhere in other countries and jurisdictions, and I do not see that our jurisdiction or country is any different from any other. This would be an incentive toward home ownership and would help people meet their housing needs. I suggest there are some suggestions I have made that should be followed up and will be of assistance, in addition to some of the provisions contained in the minister's bill.

speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I am reluctant to enter this debate because of the charm just exercised toward several members on this side of the House by the minister, who felt that it was most important that this bill receive immediate consideration by the House and sent forthwith to committee. In fact it was urged upon us on this side of the House that a great

January 29, 1975
National Housing Act
many people in this country are waiting patiently for the legislation to pass people like contractors, bankers, mortgage brokers. They are waiting patiently and with baited breath so they can trot down to the nearest bank and make a little more money.
No, Madam Speaker, I think it is very necessary that we take a careful look at what the minister is doing. At this very moment a group of people are taking a look at what the minister is doing at a meeting in the Chateau Laurier. This group represents all provinces in Canada, with the exception of New Brunswick, which is not represented at this conference.
The minister is fond of saying that consultation is so important to the political process-that it is important in keeping the country together. He has been consulting with Mr. Teron and with the mortgage companies and contractors. But I do not think he has been consulting with the poor people of this country who are looking for a meaningful housing program. I do not think he has been entering into meaningful consultations with representatives of the various provinces of this country.
By the way, Madam Speaker, it is of interest to note there is only one member of the press corps present in the press gallery at the moment. They are all over at the Chateau Laurier, because they know where the action on housing is. It is not at the federal level at all; it is at the provincial meeting at the Chateau Laurier.
A very interesting press release has been issued, and I should like to refer to some parts of it. The third item which apparently they agreed upon unanimously was that funds for social housing should meet the priority commitments of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation's budget, that these allocations should not be used to finance new or amended programs introduced by Ottawa during the budget year, but that the allocation of these priority funds should be at the discretion of individual provinces.
In other word the complaint is that when we announce new programs we abandon old programs. A mysterious sleight of hand has been taking place in the minister's department about this. Every time there is a little crisis we get another press release or headline, but we do not get any more houses.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext: We get more bandaids.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION, ETC.
speechtext:
That is right. Something else that the provinces unanimously agreed to this afternoon, according to the press release, was that current indications are that housing starts in 1975 will be only 200,000. The provinces concluded that this is too low, and they recommended a minimum target of 250,000 starts nationally, with a corresponding increase in federal dollar commitment. In other words the provinces are willing to go the extra mile. We want the federal government to show some leadership, go the extra mile and match the initiative of the provincial governments.
I was most interested to hear the remarks this afternoon of the hon. member for Matane (Mr. De Bane), who took issue with some of the figures used by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) in his address to the House yesterday. I do not think he should take issue with the

hon. member for Broadview; he should be taking issue with the Canadian Council on Social Development. That is where the figures originated, and I have complete confidence in their accuracy.
I should like to go over them again because they relate to the AHOP program and what we are talking about in this debate-the provision of housing for poor people. From these figures we learn that the average earnings level for people in the city of Vancouver to qualify under the AHOP program is $19,000 a year. You have to earn $19,000 a year before you can apply under the AHOP program. What kind of program is that? I do not qualify for an AHOP grant under the present salary level in the House of Commons; I earn only $18,000. Incidentally, my House leader makes the point that we represent a mere 1 per cent of the top income levels in the country. I do not know whether I can accept that figure, but I hope this demonstrates to the minister that this low income program is absolutely meaningless. Its provisions do not even qualify members of this House to make application under the AHOP program.
Some of the income levels in respect of these AHOP provisions are $18,000 in Ottawa, $16,000 in Halifax, $15,000 in Saint John and $14,000 in Montreal.

speechtext: Those are maximum? I suggest they are not. In any event the second point I want to make in respect of the AHOP program is that in Vancouver if you can find a house for $44,900 you can go and buy it. We have been through these figures over and over again, but let me say that I do not know of any house in the area of my ridir g where I live that is not worth more than that right now. There is almost no housing available in Vancouver under the provisions of this program.

I should like to say a word about this miracle act that came in previously, the Residential Mortgage Financing Act, which was supposed miraculously to release all this mortgage money for building houses. I think the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) said that of this group he was only able to find one that is bothering to use the provisions of that act. That is the kind of tinkering that indicates the bankruptcy of the housing policies produced by the government.
The House has been talking about the group of economic advisers in the Prime Minister's office. Apparently these economic advisers advise the minister on economic things rather than the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner).

The group of seven.

speechtext:
One member of that group is from the University of Toronto and is involved in quantitative analysis. His estimate of housing starts for this year, prior to the November budget, was 198,000. After the budget his estimate was revised to 203,450. That does not represent a very dramatic change in the estimate of housing starts for this country. On January 16, the estimate of housing starts for this year was 202,000. Of course housing starts are down 17 per cent all across the country.
At least the provinces, together and unanimously, understand this problem. They have suggested we should be building no less than 250,000 units this year, and I might say that is a pretty modest approach. The hon. member for Matane said earlier that our provincial governments are not responding. I suggest they are responding by looking for leadership and more money, but they are not getting sufficient help.
One of the key items in the increased cost of housing is the cost of land. Recently a study by the greater Vancouver regional district showed that 53 per cent of the increase in the price of houses in the lower mainland was directly the result of an increase in land prices rather than the result of increases in labour and material costs. The increase in the cost of labour and materials was responsible for about 26 per cent of the increase.
As I understand it, the amount the province of British Columbia has received from the federal government to assist in land banking and getting at this terrible problem of free enterprise speculation in land has been about $1 million. The present need is $10 million. This would indicate a sort of one-tenth response to the real problems in respect of housing in British Columbia.
We are now building a new city close to my community, for about 80,000 people. This is at least some meaningful response to the problem, but this is not a result of the leadership shown at the federal level.
Let us look at the history of what has been done in respect of housing in Canada. We used to subsidize the purchase of houses for middle income class people by guaranteeing the interest rate on loans. We still do this. Where I live almost everyone lives in one of those houses built with a loan guaranteed at an interest rate of 6 per cent or 7 per cent. The people who live in those houses are very comfortably ensconced.
The poor and the young in that community now want similar housing. Unfortunately they are meeting resistance from those middle income class people who took advantage of a subsidized program to build their excellent accommodation. They are now resisting the need for public housing. One of the reasons for this is our record of providing socialism for the rich and free enterprise for the poor. I cannot see anything in the changes proposed in the bill before us that departs from that principle of looking after the middle class first and forgetting about the low income people who so desperately need housing.
One of the main reasons for family breakups in this country is that you must have two income earners in the family in order to buy a house. With the present costs and mortgage interest rates there is no way a family with one parent at home can manage to buy a house. Both parents must work in order to meet the required payments.
National Housing Act
Our expectation with regard to housing has risen out of all proportion. Everyone aspires to the ownership of the middle class three-bedroom, three-car home. There is no longer any way we can satisfy that kind of demand in this country. We must cut down on the size of houses and the cost of housing. This will mean some pretty severe adjustments in our appetites. There are many other areas in respect of which we will have to alter our appetites as well. I suggest we must stop subsidizing the luxury housing market, and stop pouring money into that market as we have been doing.
What we have been doing is contributing to local confrontations in municipalities across the country. These confrontations are between those who are comfortably housed with mortgage rates subsidized by the government, and the poor and the young who are trying to get housing close to these attractive areas.
It is time we decided in this country, as they have in Europe, that a significant proportion of our housing program must be directed toward public housing. At the present time only 1 'A per cent of all housing in Canada is public housing. We must learn, as they have in both free enterprise and democratic socialist countries in Europe, that we can conscript capital for the purpose of public housing. This would require the banks and the lending institutions to make available a proportion of their money at interest rates of 6 per cent and 7 per cent.
I do not think there is anyone in this House who is not sympathetic to the minister because of his very difficult task in respect of housing. I know he is sincere in his desire to get housing back on the road in this country. Unfortunately he is handicapped by some pretty conservative friends in the Cabinet, in a philosophical sense, inasmuch as his portion of the federal budget is not nearly large enough to deal with this massive problem.
I hope that the minister will listen very carefully to the representations that will be made to him tomorrow at the federal-provincial conference at which the provinces have indicated their willingness to go a little farther. I hope the minister will go a little farther and commit a much more meaningful amount of money, and a more significant program in terms of land banking, public housing, and so on.
I did want to mention one other matter that I neglected to mention earlier. Under the sewer program we have a proposal for per-capita sewage grants. It would seem to me that it would be necessary, if we are serious about providing low cost housing, to tie those grants to the percentage of housing in the community going to low cost housing so that there is some commitment from the municipalities that they will pay their share in providing that kind of housing. Right now we are getting local resistance to it for the reasons I have mentioned, namely, that those of us in the middle class have been nicely looked after and we are not sufficiently in tune with the housing needs of the young and the poor. I think I have said enough, Madam Speaker.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, because of the lateness of the hour I will cut short my opening remarks and simply say that the housing

January 29, 1975
National Housing Act
problem that we now have is not only a national problem but a very intense local problem in certain areas of the country, and also a very individual problem for certain segments of our population.
There is a group of people who, because of special needs, are attracted to special locations, specific areas in our country, and I refer of course to the special needs of our senior citizens. These are people who are hurt beyond the hurt of all other segments of the population in this critical area of housing. They are people who, because of transportation needs, must live near the urban areas, and this, coincidentally is also the area of greatest cost for housing. Frequently because of health they tend to move towards the areas of Canada where the climate is more moderate, such as southern Ontario, southern B.C., Surrey-White Rock, Greater Vancouver, and Greater Victoria. It is the very attractiveness of these areas that creates the congestion. The congestion accelerates the shortage, inflates the prices, and puts these facilities out of reach of tjie people who need them the most.
But the greatest problem is that we see it as a problem. There was a time when the elderly were counted as an asset; today they are counted as a problem. Their accumulated wisdom at one time in our history was seen as a source of wealth. Their well formed opinions were seen as a force for stability. Their scope of experience was seen as a comprehension which complemented our fixation on specialization. These we considered as assets. So long as we see senior citizens as a problem we will produce half hearted solutions that tantalize rather than cure. It is no solution to invent polite euphemisms such as golden age clubs, sunset pavilions, retirement centres. Euphemisms such as that are not a cure. One hundred years ago the English poet, Robert Browning, in a poem entitled "Rabbi Ben Ezra", said:
Grow old along with me The Best Is yet to come The last of life, for which the
first was made.
I wonder how many senior citizens in our country today would be able to say with Rabbi Ben Ezra "Grow old along with me, the best is yet to come" when they are presented with a housing problem such as we have never seen before.
We have a variety of programs today for senior citizens but, no matter how they are designed, the programs always seem to end up with a housing solution that pensioners cannot afford-the payments are beyond their income, and those elderly who are on fixed income are tantalized by senior citizens' programs that are beyond their reach.
So I would like to make one suggestion to the minister to help in something that might be at least a partial solution to them, and I refer specifically to programs for non-profit senior citizens projects. Those programs are already burdened with land acquisition costs, and the private citizens who have combined resources to help senior citizens in this way have already given extensively. Yet, beyond that there is the expense of the combination of federal and provincial mortgages. In truth, there are some grants given them, but these mortgage payments are at interest rates that they cannot afford. On top of that there are property taxes. Even if the mortgage payments were such that senior citizens could afford them, there are the property taxes which the municipalities cannot afford to forgo because they need this revenue, and the property taxes help to put those projects out of reach of senior citizens.
So I would like to propose to the minister that he consider a program whereby mortgage payments on nonprofit senior citizens housing projects would be forgiven to the level of 50 per cent of the property taxes. In this way the revenue which the municipalities need would be retained for those areas. This would focus on areas of our country where the pressure in housing is the greatest on senior citizens. It would tend to alleviate the pressure in those areas; it would focus on the areas where it is felt most by senior citizens, and it would help to alleviate the pressure on that segment of the population that can least afford this kind of regular housing.
I would invite the minister to consider this proposal to forgive 50 per cent of the mortgage payments on non-profit senior citizens housing projects to the level of 50 per cent of the property taxes. I trust that this will find favour with the minister.
May I call it six o'clock, Madam Speaker?
